en: To encourage or assist someone in doing something wrong
hook: ABET: placing A BET on the criminal and helping him win.
story: Abet. During the term final, one student slipped a folded answer sheet to his friend, while the boy at the next desk kept watch for the invigilator. All three were caught. The lookout protested that he had not cheated himself. "You abetted it," said the exam committee chairman. To abet is to encourage or help someone do something wrong. Lawyers speak of aiding and abetting a crime. Abet always carries guilt: you abet a thief, never a charity.

gre.s: Although the guard never touched the jewels himself, prosecutors argued that he chose to ____ the theft by deliberately leaving the vault unlocked.
gre.clue: by deliberately leaving the vault unlocked

en: Easy to reach, use, obtain, or understand
hook: ACCESSIBLE: easy ACCESS.
story: Accessible. Professor Kamal's first physics lectures were full of equations nobody could follow. After a dismal midterm, he changed his style. He explained gravity with a falling mango and electricity with the classroom ceiling fan. Suddenly even the history students taking his course as an elective understood him. His lectures had become accessible: easy to reach, use, or understand. A building with ramps is accessible to wheelchair users. Think: access is a way in, and accessible means there is a way in.

gre.s: Unlike his dense earlier treatises, which only specialists could follow, the philosopher's final book is remarkably ____, written in plain prose for a general audience.
gre.clue: written in plain prose for a general audience

en: Excessively eager to acquire money or possessions
hook: ACQUISITIVE: always ACQUIRING more.
story: Acquisitive. Mr. Haque already owned three flats in Gulshan, two cars, and a shop in a busy market. Yet every weekend he went hunting for another plot of land, another apartment, another bargain. His children joked that he could not see anything without wanting to own it. He was deeply acquisitive: excessively eager to acquire money or possessions. The word comes from acquire, to get. An acquisitive society judges people by what they own. Synonyms: grasping, avaricious, covetous.

gre.s: Far from being content with his considerable wealth, the tycoon remained relentlessly ____, buying up rival companies merely to add them to his holdings.
gre.clue: buying up rival companies merely to add them to his holdings

en: To combine or unite into one
hook: AMALGAMATE: A MALL that GATHERs many shops into one.
story: Amalgamate. Two small banks in Chattogram were both struggling. Each had loyal customers but too little capital. Their boards met and agreed to join together as one larger bank, with a new name, one head office, and one set of accounts. They amalgamated. To amalgamate is to combine or unite into one. In chemistry, an amalgam is mercury mixed with another metal, like the silver tooth fillings dentists once used. Synonyms: merge, fuse, consolidate. Opposite: separate.

gre.s: Rather than keep the three struggling departments separate, the dean decided to ____ them into a single school with one budget and one administration.
gre.clue: into a single school with one budget and one administration

en: To reduce the force, effect, or value of; to make thin
hook: ATTENUATE: makes it THIN, TENUOUS.
story: Attenuate. Rumana's hostel room faced a road where buses honked all night. She hung a thick quilt over the window and stuffed towels under the door. The noise did not vanish, but it softened to a dull hum, and at last she slept. The quilt had attenuated the sound: reduced its force. To attenuate is to weaken, reduce, or make thin. Scientists attenuate a virus to make a safe vaccine. Think of tenuous, which also means thin and weak.

gre.s: Although the new drug does not cure the disease, it can ____ its most severe symptoms, making the illness far more bearable for patients.
gre.clue: making the illness far more bearable for patients

en: To make greater by adding to
hook: AUGMENT: like AUGMENTED reality adding layers to the world.
story: Augment. Tanvir's tuition fees swallowed most of his monthly allowance, leaving almost nothing for books. So he began teaching mathematics to two schoolchildren in the evenings. The extra eight thousand taka a month augmented his income enough to buy his GRE prep books. To augment is to make greater by adding to. You can augment a salary, a collection, or a team. Augment shares a Latin root with the name Augustus: augere, to increase. Synonyms: increase, supplement, boost.

gre.s: Because her scholarship barely covered tuition, she took a part-time job to ____ her income, adding enough each month to pay the rent.
gre.clue: adding enough each month to pay the rent

en: A strong dislike or disinclination
hook: AVERSION: you AVERT (turn away) your eyes from it.
story: Aversion. Ishita loves almost every Bangladeshi dish except bitter gourd. Since childhood, the sight of karela on her plate makes her push it away. Her mother tried frying it crisp, mixing it with potatoes, even hiding it in dal. Ishita still found it and refused. She has a strong aversion to it: a deep dislike. Aversion is usually followed by to: an aversion to crowds, an aversion to risk. Think of averse, turning away. Synonyms: distaste, antipathy, repugnance.

gre.s: The novelist's lifelong ____ to publicity explains why, despite her enormous commercial success, she has given almost no interviews.
gre.clue: she has given almost no interviews

en: Cheerfully carefree; casually indifferent to something serious
hook: BLITHE: BLISSfully unaware.
story: Blithe. Two days before his thesis was due, Shuvo was still singing in the hostel corridor, playing carrom, and planning a trip to Cox's Bazar. His roommate panicked on his behalf. Shuvo just smiled and said everything would work out. His attitude was blithe: cheerfully carefree, but dangerously indifferent to something serious. A blithe dismissal of a warning cheerfully ignores real danger. Blithe sounds light, like a bird singing, and that lightness is the point. Synonyms: carefree, nonchalant, heedless.

gre.s: The CEO's ____ dismissal of the auditors' warnings, delivered with a cheerful wave of the hand, alarmed investors who knew how serious the losses were.
gre.clue: delivered with a cheerful wave of the hand

en: The feeling that someone or something is worthless or beneath consideration
hook: CONTEMPT: CON + TEMPT; you're not even tempted to respect it.
story: Contempt. At a wedding in Dhaka, a wealthy guest snapped his fingers at the young waiter, never once looking at his face, and complained loudly that people like him should be grateful for any work. Everyone at the table felt the sting. His tone showed contempt: the feeling that someone is worthless or beneath consideration. Contempt of court means disrespecting a judge's authority. The proverb says familiarity breeds contempt. Synonyms: scorn, disdain, derision. Opposite: respect.

gre.s: Far from offering measured criticism, the reviewer made no attempt to hide her ____ for the film, dismissing it as unworthy of even a single serious paragraph.
gre.clue: dismissing it as unworthy of even a single serious paragraph

en: To waste time; to be slow
hook: DAWDLE: like a DOODLE, wasting time drawing nothing.
story: Dawdle. Babu was sent to the bazaar to buy fish for lunch. On the way he stopped to watch a cricket match, chatted with the tea seller, and spent twenty minutes admiring a new motorbike. He came home at two o'clock, and his mother had already cooked dal and rice without him. "Stop dawdling," she said. To dawdle is to waste time or move slowly. Students dawdle before starting homework. Synonyms: dally, linger, loiter. Opposite: hasten.

gre.s: With the deadline only hours away, the team could not afford to ____; every minute spent idling would make the final report weaker.
gre.clue: every minute spent idling

en: To cause something to change direction; to avoid
bn: বিচ্যুত করা; ভিন্ন দিকে ফিরিয়ে দেওয়া
hook: DEFLECT: like a shield DEFLECTING an arrow.
story: Deflect. At a press conference, a reporter asked the minister about missing flood relief funds. The minister smiled and began talking about the new metro rail. The reporter asked again; the minister praised the national cricket team. He had deflected the question: turned it aside without answering. To deflect is to make something change direction, or to avoid it. A goalkeeper deflects a shot over the bar. Think: de means away, and flect means bend, so deflect means bend away.

gre.s: Rather than address the allegations directly, the spokesperson tried to ____ them, steering every question back toward the company's charitable work.
gre.clue: steering every question back toward the company's charitable work

en: To regard as unimportant or untrustworthy; to disregard
hook: GRE trick: DISCOUNT means to ignore, not just lower the price.
story: Discount. Mitu's grandmother has diabetes. When a neighbour insisted that bitter lemon water could replace her insulin, the doctor did not argue. He simply discounted the advice and kept her on her medicine. Some claims deserve to be discounted: regarded as unimportant or untrustworthy, and set aside. In a shop, a discount reduces the price; in an argument, discounting a claim reduces its weight to almost nothing. Never discount a theory just because it is new. Synonyms: disregard, dismiss.

gre.s: Scientists were quick to ____ the anonymous report, since its author offered no data and had a long history of fabricating results.
gre.clue: had a long history of fabricating results

en: A person who opposes official policy, especially of an authoritarian state
hook: DIS-SIDE-ent: on the other SIDE.
story: Dissident. Under a military regime, a young journalist kept publishing articles that criticised the generals, even after her newspaper was shut down. She printed leaflets at night, was arrested twice, and finally had to flee the country. Yet her essays kept circulating. She was a dissident: a person who openly opposes official policy, especially in an authoritarian state. Dissident comes from dissent, to disagree. As an adjective, we speak of dissident voices or dissident writers. Opposite: loyalist.

gre.s: The regime claimed to tolerate free speech, yet any ____ who criticized its policies in print could expect to be imprisoned or forced into exile.
gre.clue: who criticized its policies in print

en: Successful in producing the desired result; effective
hook: EFFICACIOUS: EFFECTIVE.
story: Efficacious. In the nineteen sixties and seventies, cholera and diarrhoea killed huge numbers of children in Bangladesh. Researchers in Dhaka helped show that a cheap drink of clean water, salt, and sugar could keep these children alive. Oral saline proved astonishingly efficacious: successful in producing the desired result. Efficacious is a formal word for effective, used mostly of treatments, methods, and policies. The noun is efficacy. Synonyms: effective, potent, successful. Opposite: ineffectual.

gre.s: The manufacturer touted the supplement as highly ____, yet independent trials showed that it relieved symptoms no better than a sugar pill.
gre.clue: relieved symptoms no better than a sugar pill

en: Fair and impartial
hook: EQUITABLE: EQUAL for all.
story: Equitable. When their father died, three brothers in a Rajshahi village had to divide his mango orchard. The eldest wanted the biggest share. Their uncle walked the land, counted the trees, and drew the lines so that each brother received the same number of fruiting trees and equal access to the pond. Everyone agreed the division was equitable: fair and impartial. Equitable shares a root with equal and equity. Synonyms: fair, just, even-handed. Opposite: biased.

gre.s: Critics argued that the new tax was hardly ____, since it fell most heavily on the poorest families while leaving the wealthy almost untouched.
gre.clue: fell most heavily on the poorest families while leaving the wealthy almost untouched

en: Not regular or predictable; inconsistent
hook: ERRATIC: full of ERRORS, all over the place.
story: Erratic. Electricity in Joya's village came and went without any pattern. Some days it stayed on all evening; other days it vanished at noon, returned for ten minutes, and vanished again. Nobody could plan anything. The supply was erratic: irregular and unpredictable. Behaviour can be erratic too, like a driver swerving between lanes for no reason. Erratic shares a root with error and errant, meaning to wander. Synonyms: inconsistent, unpredictable, capricious. Opposite: steady.

gre.s: The athlete's performances have been so ____ this season, brilliant one week and dismal the next, that even her coaches cannot predict how she will do.
gre.clue: brilliant one week and dismal the next

en: Hardworking and diligent
hook: INDUSTRIOUS: works like a whole INDUSTRY.
story: Industrious. Farhan's mother runs a small tailoring shop in Mirpur. She opens at seven, sews until midnight during the Eid rush, keeps careful accounts, and still checks her son's homework. Neighbours say they have never once seen her idle. She is industrious: hardworking and diligent. Do not confuse it with industrial, which relates to factories. An industrious person works hard; an industrial zone has factories. Synonyms: diligent, assiduous, sedulous. Opposite: indolent.

gre.s: Though he had a reputation for laziness as a student, as an apprentice he proved remarkably ____, often staying at the workshop long after everyone else had gone home.
gre.clue: often staying at the workshop long after everyone else had gone home

en: To give information to; also, to give an essential quality to or influence
bn: জানানো; প্রভাবিত করা, বৈশিষ্ট্য দান করা
hook: GRE trick: experience INFORMS art means it SHAPES it from within.
story: Inform. Priya grew up in a fishing village near the Sundarbans, watching her father mend nets and survive cyclones. Years later, as an architect, she designed storm shelters for coastal towns. Every drawing carried what she had learned as a child about wind, water, and fear. Her childhood informed her work: it gave the work its essential quality and shaped it. Usually inform means to tell. On the GRE, it often means to shape or permeate, as in faith informs her poetry.

gre.s: Her years as a war correspondent continue to ____ her fiction: nearly every novel she writes returns to scenes of conflict and displacement.
gre.clue: nearly every novel she writes returns to scenes of conflict and displacement

en: Irritating; annoying
hook: IRKSOME: something that IRKS you.
story: Irksome. Sabbir's new flatmate had one small habit: he cracked his knuckles every few minutes, loudly, while Sabbir tried to study. It was not a serious problem, but by the end of the week Sabbir could think of nothing else. The habit was irksome: irritating and annoying. Irksome comes from irk, to annoy, and suggests small, repeated irritations rather than real harm. Long queues and slow internet are irksome. Synonyms: vexing, tiresome, galling.

gre.s: What began as a minor inconvenience grew increasingly ____ over the months, until the constant construction noise drove several tenants to move out.
gre.clue: drove several tenants to move out

en: A metal band for chaining someone's hands; to restrain
hook: MAN-ACLE: shackles on a MAN's hands (manus).
story: Manacle. In a history museum, Lamia stopped before a glass case holding a pair of rusted iron manacles: two thick rings joined by a chain, once locked around a prisoner's wrists. The guide explained that the word comes from Latin manus, hand, as in manual. A manacle is an old handcuff. As a verb, to manacle is to chain or restrain. Figuratively, debt or tradition can manacle a person. Synonyms: shackle, fetter. Opposite: liberate.

gre.s: Rather than liberating the workers, the new contracts seemed designed to ____ them, binding them to the company with debts they could never repay.
gre.clue: binding them to the company with debts they could never repay

en: Humble about one's achievements; moderate in size or amount
hook: MODEST: MODERATE, not boastful, not extreme.
story: Modest. Nadia scored in the top one percent on her GRE. When relatives praised her at dinner, she only said she had been lucky with the reading passages, and changed the subject to her cousin's wedding. She was modest: humble about her achievements. Modest also means moderate in size or amount: a modest salary, a modest flat, a modest improvement. On the GRE, watch for this second sense. Opposites: boastful for people, and substantial or lavish for amounts.

gre.s: Despite the company's grand promises of transformation, the new policy produced only ____ gains, raising productivity by barely two percent.
gre.clue: raising productivity by barely two percent

en: Harmful, poisonous, or very unpleasant
hook: NOXIOUS: like NOX, toxic gas.
story: Noxious. Near the old tanneries of Hazaribagh, the canal water once ran blue and black, and the air carried a sharp chemical smell that made visitors cover their faces. Residents complained of rashes and constant coughing. The fumes were noxious: harmful, poisonous, or very unpleasant. Noxious comes from Latin noxa, harm. Its cousin innocent literally means harmless. We speak of noxious gases, noxious weeds, even noxious ideas. Synonyms: toxic, harmful, poisonous. Opposite: wholesome.

gre.s: The factory insisted its emissions were harmless, yet residents downwind reported headaches and nausea whenever the ____ fumes drifted over the town.
gre.clue: reported headaches and nausea

en: Having a harmful effect, especially gradually or subtly
hook: PERNICIOUS: slowly PERISHING you.
story: Pernicious. Rafi started checking his phone for just a minute before studying. A month later, that minute had become three hours a night, his grades had slipped, and he could not read a page without reaching for the screen. The habit never seemed dangerous on any single day; its harm grew quietly. It was pernicious: harmful, especially in a gradual or subtle way. Noxious harm is obvious, like poison gas; pernicious harm creeps in unnoticed. Synonyms: insidious, destructive.

gre.s: The rumors were all the more ____ for being subtle: no single falsehood seemed serious, yet together they slowly destroyed public trust in the institution.
gre.clue: yet together they slowly destroyed public trust

en: A difficult, unpleasant, or embarrassing situation
hook: PREDICAMENT: a PREDICTION gone wrong, now you're stuck.
story: Predicament. Zayan reached Kamalapur station with five minutes to spare, then realised his wallet was gone. No ticket, no money, a dead phone, and his exam in Sylhet was the next morning. He stood on the platform, wondering whom he could possibly ask for help. He was in a real predicament: a difficult, unpleasant, or embarrassing situation. A predicament usually has no easy way out. Synonyms: plight, quandary, dilemma, fix. Opposite: a windfall or a stroke of luck.

gre.s: Stranded abroad after their airline collapsed, and with no money to buy new tickets, the tourists faced a grim ____ that their embassy was slow to resolve.
gre.clue: Stranded abroad after their airline collapsed

en: Competent and skilled in an activity or area of knowledge
hook: PROFICIENT: as skilled as a PRO.
story: Proficient. When Anika joined a software company, she could barely write a working program. She practised every night, solved hundreds of coding problems, and asked senior colleagues endless questions. Two years later, the newest interns came to her for help. She had become proficient: competent and skilled. It is usually followed by in or at: proficient in English, proficient at chess. Proficient comes from a Latin verb meaning to make progress. Synonyms: adept, skilled, accomplished. Opposite: inept.

gre.s: Although she had studied Spanish for only a year, she was already so ____ that native speakers often assumed she had grown up in Madrid.
gre.clue: native speakers often assumed she had grown up in Madrid

en: Using too many words; tediously lengthy
hook: PROLIX: PRO at being LONG.
story: Prolix. The chief guest at the school prize-giving was supposed to speak for five minutes. He spoke for fifty. He repeated every point three times, told stories that led nowhere, and thanked each teacher by name, twice. The students fell asleep in rows. His speech was prolix: using too many words, tediously lengthy. Think: prolix speeches are prolonged. Synonyms: verbose, wordy, long-winded. Opposites: terse, concise, laconic.

gre.s: The editor urged the author to cut the manuscript in half, complaining that its ____ style buried every interesting idea under pages of needless detail.
gre.clue: buried every interesting idea under pages of needless detail

en: Strong contempt; to reject with contempt
hook: SCORN: SCORE zero on respect.
story: Scorn. When Mahin announced that he would leave his engineering degree to become a potter, his relatives laughed at the dinner table. "Making clay pots? After all that education?" they said with scorn. Five years later, his ceramics sell in galleries in Dhaka and Singapore. Scorn is strong contempt. As a verb, to scorn is to reject or treat with contempt: to scorn advice, to scorn an offer. Synonyms: disdain, derision, contempt. Opposite: admiration.

gre.s: Purists tend to ____ any adaptation of a classic novel, dismissing even the most faithful film versions as cheap imitations.
gre.clue: dismissing even the most faithful film versions as cheap imitations

en: Lower in rank or importance; to treat as less important
hook: SUB-ORDINATE: ranked (ordered) BELOW.
story: Subordinate. In Tania's office, the junior officers wait until the director has spoken before they say anything. They are his subordinates: lower in rank. But Tania noticed something else. When the director planned the year's budget, he cut staff training to buy new leather chairs. He had subordinated learning to comfort, treating it as less important. As a verb, to subordinate is to rank something below something else. As an adjective, subordinate to means beneath. Opposite: superior.

gre.s: In the director's view, every other goal was ____ to profit: any project that failed to raise revenue was promptly cancelled.
gre.clue: any project that failed to raise revenue was promptly cancelled

en: Not proper or appropriate; in bad taste
hook: UN-SEEMLY: doesn't SEEM right.
story: Unseemly. At a funeral in Sylhet, two cousins began arguing loudly over who would inherit the family house, while the body still lay in the courtyard. The elders hushed them, ashamed. Such a quarrel at such a moment was unseemly: improper and in bad taste. Unseemly does not mean ugly; it means not fitting the occasion. Think: it does not seem right. Synonyms: indecorous, unbecoming, inappropriate. Opposite: decorous.

gre.s: Many guests found the candidate's lavish victory party ____, since it took place just hours after deadly floods had devastated the region.
gre.clue: just hours after deadly floods had devastated the region

en: Real; used to emphasize that a description is accurate
hook: VERITABLE: VERY TRUE (veritas = truth).
story: Veritable. Sara opened her grandfather's old trunk expecting dusty clothes. Instead she found letters from 1971, black and white photographs of freedom fighters, a hand-drawn map of their village, and a diary covering forty years. It was a veritable treasure trove of family history. Veritable emphasizes that a description, even a dramatic one, is truly accurate. Think of verity, meaning truth, as in verify. A veritable feast, a veritable genius. Synonyms: real, genuine, true.

gre.s: The once-neglected archive has become a ____ goldmine for historians: scholars have already uncovered hundreds of documents previously thought lost.
gre.clue: scholars have already uncovered hundreds of documents previously thought lost
